comments.author: participant3
comments.body:
I tracked this down to `bevy_ecs_path`.

```diff
  pub(crate) fn bevy_ecs_path() -> syn::Path {
-     BevyManifest::default().get_path("bevy_ecs")
+     BevyManifest::shared().get_path("bevy_ecs")
  }
```

The difference seems to be that before 760d0a31003c70ed6017b2a70059a76d9b268425, this function returned `bevy_internal::ecs`, and now it returns `bevy_ecs`.

comments.author: participant5
comments.body: I have thought about it quite a bit by now. RA seems to keep the proc macros server running and only alters the environment variables. This I did not account for. It should be possible to do a workaround in stable rust by using a HashMap of LazyLocked BevyManifests to look up which crate RA invoked the proc macros for. But to justify this added complexity build performance should be benchmarked.

comments.author: participant6
comments.body:
> maybe a bug in how rust-analyser share context between executions? `BevyManifest` is now behind a `LazyLock` which is not an issue in normal compilation, but it seems RA keeps it across crates

I wouldn't call it a bug. rust-analyzer caches proc-macro expansions keyed by their invocation inputs, unlike rustc (which is currently experimenting with caching derives fwiw). proc-macros generally shouldn't rely on global state like this as even rustc doesn't make a guarantee about the order or frequency of proc-macro invocations.

> However there is a nightly feature for tracked path and tracked environment variables in nightly that should guarantee the external state dependence.

Those are not implemented in rust-analyzer yet.

> I have thought about it quite a bit by now. RA seems to keep the proc macros server running and only alters the environment variables. 

Yes, we keep the proc-macro library loaded (so `static`s do not get reset), we do spawn a new thread per expansion though (so thread locals do get reset). So an easy fix here would be to use a thread local instead of a `static`, though the better fix really would be to not cache anything inside globals in the first place.

comments.author: participant7

> benchmark the build performance

Maybe you could make a small crate that depends on `bevy_ecs` and has a ton of component declarations (or other macro invocations), then run `hyperfine "touch src/main.rs; cargo check"`.

I don't think you'll see much of a regression though.

comments.author: participant3
comments.body: Thanks, I'll try that.

comments.author: participant3
comments.body:
I used this source code with 10.000 components for the benchmark:

```rust
use bevy_ecs::component::Component;

#[derive(Component)]
struct C0000;

#[derive(Component)]
struct C0001;

// ...

#[derive(Component)]
struct C9998;

#[derive(Component)]
struct C9999;

fn main() {}
```

Running `hyperfine --warmup 10 --prepare 'touch src/main.rs' 'cargo check'` yielded the following results:

**My bug fix (#17310)**

```text
Benchmark 1: cargo check
  Time (mean ± σ):      3.922 s ±  0.034 s    [User: 3.551 s, System: 0.366 s]
  Range (min … max):    3.865 s …  3.966 s    10 runs
```

**760d0a31003c70ed6017b2a70059a76d9b268425 reverted**

```text
Benchmark 1: cargo check
  Time (mean ± σ):      4.788 s ±  0.041 s    [User: 4.341 s, System: 0.442 s]
  Range (min … max):    4.734 s …  4.854 s    10 runs
```

**Current (incorrect) implementation** for reference

```text
Benchmark 1: cargo check
  Time (mean ± σ):      3.878 s ±  0.032 s    [User: 3.516 s, System: 0.356 s]
  Range (min … max):    3.851 s …  3.936 s    10 runs
```

My conclusion is that my fix does provide a performance benefit over reverting 760d0a31003c70ed6017b2a70059a76d9b268425, and is in fact close in performance to the current incorrect implementation.
